newsitem.title: USA: Sony Pictures chief Levine steps down.
newsitem.headline: Sony Pictures chief Levine steps down.

text.p: Sony Corp. said Wednesday that Alan Levine resigned as president and chief operating officer of Sony Pictures Entertainment, capping months of management turmoil at the troubled studio.
In a terse statement, Sony said Levine has agreed to stay on for a brief transition period.
Sony did not name a replacement for Levine but the company confirmed it was in talks with United Artists President John Calley about taking a senior studio job.
It was not immediately clear if Calley would assume all of the duties previously performed by Levine or if he would share some responsibilities with other Sony executives.

According to people familar with Levine's decision, the move came after he met with Sony Corp. President and Chief Operating Officer Nobuyuki Idei in New York Tuesday in hopes of securing a vote of confidence.
However, when Idei suggested Levine share responsibilty with Calley, Levine submitted his resignation.
In a statement Idei thanked Levine for guiding the company through a difficult period.

"We greatly appreciate Alan's leadership of SPE over the past two years, as well as his long term contribution to Sony," Idei said. "He has been instrumental in a complex transition and restructuring at SPE, and has solidly positioned the studio for the next stage in its worldwide growth and evolution."
Levine's departure had been widely expected after Sony's dismal performance at the box office this summer.

A former entertainment attorney who once said he wanted to run a major studio since he was 12, Levine ran into trouble earlier this year when several films flopped at the box office and relations between him and studio boss Mark Canton became strained.

In September, Levine finally fired Canton. But his choice for Canton's replacement, William Morris talent agent Arnold Rifkin, was voted down by Idei, prompting many in Hollywood to suggest Levine's tenure at Sony was shortlived.
The departure of Levine and Canton marks the latest in a series of high-level resignations this year at the studio, which Sony purchased in 1989 for $3.4 billion.

Earlier this summer, Marc Platt, president of Sony's TriStar Pictures, left to take a job at Universal Pictures and Lisa Henson, president of Sony's Columbia Pictures, stepped down to form her own production company.
In addition, Sid Ganis, the head of Sony Pictures marketing unit, also stepped down.

Analysts said Levine earned high marks for cutting Sony's costs and restoring the studio to profitability. But, with most of the gains coming from television programs like "Jeopardy!" rather than the studio's film division, the pressure to deliver a box office hit intensified.

Seeking to silence the critics, Sony agreed to pay comedian Jim Carrey $20 million to star in "The Cable Guy", a dark comedy that Levine and Canton were banking on to be one of the summer's biggest hits. The gamble proved to be embarrassing when the film opened to half-empty theaters.
Levine's departure raises questions about whether anyone can turn the troubled studio around.

Analysts said Calley, who helped revive United Artists with such hits as the James Bond film "Golden Eye" and "Leaving Las Vegas" could end up being a "caretaker" of sorts, helping the studio regain its footing so Sony could pursue a sale of at least part of the studio.
In 1994, Sony posted a $3.2 billion loss on its entertainment operation, leading to the departure of Peter Guber and Jon Peters.
Last year, Sony's management ranks were rattled again when Idei dismissed its most senior U.S. executive, Sony Corp. of America Chief Michael Schulhof.
